newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish Foreign Minister attacks "lies and smears".
newsitem.headline: Irish Foreign Minister attacks "lies and smears".

text.p: Irish Foreign Minister Ray Burke, a key figure in the Northern Ireland peace process, said on Thursday he was the victim of a smear campaign over a 30,000 Irish pounds ($43,000) political contribution.

Burke, in office for less than two months, said in a statement he was the "target of a vicious campaign of rumour and innuendo" and said police were examining "a number of anonymous threatening letters" over the affair.

Burke is the Irish representative in the Northern Ireland peace process, co-sponsored by Britain, which moves into its first substantive negotiations on September 15 in search of a resolution to the 28-year conflict.

It was the second time in a month that payments to politicians had become front-page Irish news, after former prime minister Charles Haughey admitted to an official tribunal that he had received 1.3 million pounds from chain store tycoon Ben Dunne.

The Haughey affair shocked the nation and led to calls from the opposition for a thorough investigation of Haughey's financial affairs and those of the Fianna Fail party, which leads a minority government after June 6 elections.
Burke, a member of Fianna Fail like Haughey and current Prime Minister Bertie Ahern, said he had received 30,000 pounds in 1989 "as a totally unsolicited political contribution".
He said it came from Michael Bailey of Bovale Developments and James Gogarty, an executive of Joseph Murphy Structural Engineers (JMSE).
Burke said he knew Bailey, whom his statement referred to as a "resident of North Dublin and a long time supporter of Fianna Fail". He said he had not met Gogarty before.

"Mr Gogarty told me that JMSE wished to make a political contribution to me and I received from him, in good faith, a sum of 30,000 pounds as a totally unsolicited political contribution," Burke said.

"At no time during our meeting were any favours sought or given. For the record, I have never done any favours for or made any representations to anyone on behalf of JMSE, Michael Bailey, Bovale Developments or Mr James Gogarty either before or since 1989," the statement said.
Burke specifically denied allegations in the London Sunday Times, which has an Irish edition, that he received 80,000 pounds.
"I am taking the opportunity to state unequivocally that I have done nothing illegal, unethical or improper. Indeed, I find myself the victim of a campaign of calumny and abuse," he said.
The contribution to Burke has received wide coverage in the wake of the Haughey affair.
Haughey's case came to light when former transport minister Michael Lowry resigned last year after admitting Dunne paid for the quarter-million pound renovation of his private home.

The admission led to the setting-up of a tribunal into payments to politicians after it emerged that all major political parties had received money from Dunne, whose family owns the Dunnes Stores high street department store chain.

Haughey at first denied having received any money. Later, though, he told the tribunal the money had been given to him between 1989 and 1992 but he knew nothing about it because his financial affairs were handled by a colleague who has since died.
Ahern has said he will wait to see what the tribunal recommends when it finishes its work before calling for any new investigation into financial contributions to Haughey or anyone else.
The affair has led to calls for a probe of the links between politics and big business, and a code of practice for government political contributions. ($ = 0.697 Irish Pounds)
